title: Let out a backpack strap at its ladder lock: hold the buckle tipped up while drawing the webbing through
instruction: Lengthen the near shoulder strap of the backpack until its loose end sticks out only 7 cm past the buckle, and leave the buckle holding.
context: Almost everyone carries a backpack and resets its shoulder straps. On a daypack each strap adjusts at a ladder-lock buckle on the lower end of the padded strap, where 25 mm webbing from the bag's bottom corner runs through it. Pulling the loose end tightens the strap; letting it out needs the buckle's tab lifted. A buckle maker puts it as "Created to hold under tension, then release by lifting the tab" (Country Brook Design). Off the shoulders this takes two hands: one holds the buckle tipped up off the webbing (let go, it lies back down and grips), the other draws the webbing through it from the bag side by the right amount; then the buckle is laid flat so that it holds. Pulled without the tab lifted, the strap does not give and the bag is dragged along.
setup: A table in front of two arms (bases 61 cm apart), seen by one overhead camera and a camera on each wrist. Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases: x forward (away from the arms), y to the robot's left. An empty school daypack (30 x 44 cm, 0.45 kg, 600D polyester with a grey air-mesh back panel) lies face down and loose on the table at x 11 to 41, y -25.5 to 18.5, its back panel 8.5 cm up and its top toward the robot's left. Two red padded shoulder straps (6 cm wide, 1.2 cm thick foam), joined by a sternum strap, lie on the panel along y from its top edge down to y 7, at x 20 (the near strap, the one to adjust) and x 32. At the lower end of each, a webbing tab is sewn round the end bar of a black acetal 25 mm ladder-lock buckle (35 x 26 mm, 6.5 mm tall, 5 g; the near one's centre bar at x 20, y 3). A black nylon webbing (25 mm wide, 1.6 mm thick), sewn to the panel near its bottom corner (stitched over y -22.5 to -21), runs 24 cm up the panel to the buckle, through it and over its centre bar, and back out under the buckle's lift tab; its loose end, its tip folded and stitched, lies on top of the webbing and sticks out 15 cm past the buckle's tab edge (to y -13.3). The buckle tips about its centre bar and the webbing bends; everything else is part of the backpack. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot.
scoring: The simulation reports the buckle's angle off the webbing, how far webbing has been drawn through it (the strap let out; the loose end is 15 cm minus that past the buckle's tab edge), the backpack's position, and each gripper's centre from the arm's joints. The backpack pulled off the table (its middle 3 cm or more below where it lay) sets the score to 0 for the rest of the run; sliding it on the table costs nothing. Otherwise partial credit is the best stage reached: 0.25 the strap let out by 2 cm or more; 0.5 let out by 7 to 9 cm (the loose end 6 to 8 cm past the buckle); 0.75 that with the buckle laid back flat (within 15 degrees of the webbing), so that it grips. 1.0: let out by 7 to 9 cm, the buckle flat, both grippers 5 cm or more from the buckle and from the webbing, everything still for 1 s. Doing nothing scores 0. On a real backpack: the loose end measured with a tape from the buckle's tab edge to its tip, the buckle lying flat on the webbing in a photo, the backpack still on the table.
reset_notes: Pull the near strap's loose end until it sticks out 15 cm past the buckle's tab edge (pulling the loose end tightens the strap without lifting the tab), lay the webbing straight along the panel with the loose end on top of it, and set the backpack back on its tape marks, as in the screenshot. In the simulation each trial starts the simulator afresh (each inspect-robots run does).
fidelity: Rigid bodies (PhysX), 20 Hz. Backpack (rigid, loose), buckle and webbing at true size; the webbing is a chain of rigid 15 mm links on springy hinges (no twist). Its wrap over the buckle's centre bar is not simulated: it runs on under the padded strap to a hidden slide that pulls the tail in as far. The grip is a rule from the buckle's angle: held within 30 degrees of the webbing, 1.5 N of friction past 50; a spring returns the buckle flat. Pulling the tail does not tighten the strap.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0 (the right gripper went to the near strap's sewn bottom corner and hovered over the webbing there; the left arm stayed back and the buckle was never lifted); demo: 1.0
